engine.name: A.R.I.A. Decision Engine
engine.purpose: Govern operational decisions that require an authorized choice between materially different paths. The engine determines when a decision exists, what options are available, what evidence and consequences matter, who has authority to decide, when the decision becomes time-sensitive, and what downstream work depends on the outcome.
principles: A decision is not the same as a task.
A question is not automatically a decision.
A.R.I.A. should distinguish execution choices from decisions requiring authority.
Decision support should clarify options rather than manufacture certainty.
A.R.I.A. should identify material consequences of each supported option.
Unknown consequences must remain unknown rather than invented.
A preferred recommendation must remain distinguishable from the authorized decision.
Decision authority must not be invented.
An unresolved decision may block or threaten downstream work.
A decision should be made early enough to preserve meaningful options when timing matters.
The chosen option may create new obligations, dependencies, commitments, or conflicts.
Decision history must remain explainable and provenance-preserving.

applicable_conditions: multiple materially different execution paths exist
a conflict requires an authorized choice
commitment protection requires renegotiation or displacement
new information changes the available options
a previously made decision must be reconsidered

needs_information.description: A decision exists, but materially necessary information is still missing.

ready.description: Sufficient information exists for the authorized decision-maker to make a useful decision.

pending.description: The decision is awaiting action from the authorized decision-maker.

at_risk.description: Delay in deciding is materially reducing available options or threatening downstream obligations.

decided.description: An authorized choice has been made.

implemented.description: The selected decision has been translated into the required operational actions.

reconsideration_required.description: Material new information or changed conditions justify re-evaluating a prior decision.

superseded.description: Another supported decision or changed condition has replaced the original decision requirement.

cancelled.description: The decision is no longer required.

unresolved.description: Available information is insufficient to determine current decision state.

decision_types.priority_tradeoff: Choose which valid obligation should receive scarce execution opportunity.
decision_types.resource_allocation: Choose how constrained people, crews, equipment, funding, or other resources should be allocated.
decision_types.schedule: Choose between materially different execution timing options.
decision_types.scope: Choose what work, deliverable, or outcome should be included or excluded.
decision_types.technical: Choose between materially different technical approaches requiring operational authority.
decision_types.commercial: Choose a business, pricing, purchasing, vendor, or commercial path.
decision_types.customer: Choose a customer-facing response, concession, commitment, or action.
decision_types.personnel: Choose an assignment, staffing, responsibility, or personnel-related operational path.
decision_types.risk: Choose whether and how to accept, reduce, transfer, or avoid a supported operational risk.
decision_types.commitment: Choose how to handle an existing or proposed commitment.
decision_types.conflict_resolution: Choose a path for resolving incompatible valid obligations or constraints.
decision_types.escalation: Choose whether or how to increase handling authority or intervention.
decision_types.other: A supported operational decision not represented by another canonical type.

questions: Is there more than one materially different legitimate path?
Does choosing among those paths require authority rather than ordinary execution judgment?
Will the choice materially affect outcome, timing, cost, risk, commitment, scope, customer, or downstream work?
Who has authority to make the choice?
When must the decision be made to preserve useful options?
rules: Routine execution judgment should not be unnecessarily promoted into a formal decision.
A preference does not become a decision requirement unless a choice must actually be made.
A.R.I.A. should identify the specific question that needs resolution.
Decision scope should be narrow enough to support a clear choice.
Unknown decision authority must remain unknown rather than invented.

requirements: Each materially independent decision should have a persistent identity.
The decision question must be explicit enough to evaluate options.
Recommendation and selected decision must remain distinguishable.
Decision authority must reference supported authority information when available.
Decision history must remain recoverable after implementation.

rules: Options should represent materially different choices rather than cosmetic variations.
Infeasible options should remain identifiable when useful but must not be presented as equally viable.
Unknown effects should remain unknown.
A.R.I.A. should avoid false precision when comparing options.
Evidence supporting option effects should remain traceable when materially relevant.
A.R.I.A. should identify information that would materially improve the decision.
Missing information should only delay the decision when its value is material.
The system should not chase perfect information when delay creates greater consequence.
Information requirements may become dependencies.
Follow-Up Engine may govern pursuit of missing decision information.
A.R.I.A. should identify when a decision can reasonably proceed despite uncertainty.

recommendation.purpose: Allow A.R.I.A. to recommend a decision without confusing recommendation with authority.
rules: A.R.I.A. may recommend an option when available evidence supports a preference.
The recommendation should identify the material reasons for the preference.
Recommendation confidence should reflect evidence quality and uncertainty.
A.R.I.A. must not represent its recommendation as the user's decision.
A.R.I.A. must not manufacture a recommendation when options are materially indistinguishable or evidence is insufficient.
Where useful, A.R.I.A. should identify what would change the recommendation.
Decision timing should reflect when the choice must be made, not merely the final work deadline.
A decision may become urgent before execution becomes urgent.
A.R.I.A. should identify the latest useful decision point when reasonably determinable.
Passing the useful decision point may reduce available options or increase consequence.
A closing decision window may trigger Priority, Attention, Conflict, Scheduling, Capacity, Commitment, or Escalation reevaluation.
Unknown timing must not be fabricated.
Decision authority should be based on supported organizational, contractual, workflow, ownership, or explicit authority information.
A.R.I.A. must not infer authority solely from seniority, job title, email presence, or prior participation.
A.R.I.A. should distinguish recommendation authority from final decision authority.
Where multiple authorities are required, all required approvals should remain visible.
Unresolved authority may itself become a dependency or escalation condition.
A decision is not implemented merely because it was made.
The selected option should create or update the operational work required for execution.
Implementation tasks should be routed through Capture Engine when new obligations exist.
Commitment changes resulting from the decision must be governed by Commitment Engine.
Delegation changes must be governed by Delegation Engine.
Schedule changes must be governed by Scheduling Engine.
Resolution of the decision work item must not silently resolve unrelated implementation work.
Reconsideration should preserve the original decision and rationale.
A prior decision should not be reopened merely because another option later appears preferable in hindsight.
Material changed conditions may justify a new decision record or linked decision revision.
Reconsideration must remain distinguishable from ordinary execution adjustment.
Priority Engine determines the operational importance of the decision and affected work.
Decision Engine determines what choice must be made.
High priority does not automatically determine which option should be selected.
Decision consequences may provide new factors for Priority reevaluation.
Decision Engine must not independently overwrite canonical priority.
Decision Engine determines whether a decision is identified, ready, pending, or at risk.
Attention Engine determines when and how the decision should be presented to the user.
A decision requiring the user's unique authority may deserve direct attention.
A decision should not repeatedly consume attention while materially necessary information is still being gathered unless intervention is useful.
Dependency Engine governs prerequisite conditions.
A decision may itself be a dependency for downstream work.
Missing decision information may become dependencies.
Making the decision may satisfy a decision dependency but does not complete downstream work.
Conflict Engine identifies materially incompatible obligations or constraints.
Decision Engine governs the authorized choice required to resolve conflicts when a choice is necessary.
Not every conflict requires a formal decision.
A decision resolving one conflict may create another and should trigger reevaluation when appropriate.
Capacity Engine determines practical execution capacity.
Decision Engine may use capacity findings when evaluating resource-allocation or tradeoff options.
A decision must not assume unavailable capacity.
Adding capacity as a selected option must remain operationally plausible.
Scheduling Engine determines practical execution timing.
Decision Engine may govern choices between materially different schedule paths.
A scheduling recommendation is not automatically a decision.
A selected schedule option must be implemented through Scheduling Engine.
Commitment Engine governs promises and commitment state.
Decision Engine may evaluate choices that affect commitments.
Selecting an option does not silently modify an existing commitment.
Any renegotiation or new promise must remain governed by Commitment Engine.
Delegation Engine governs execution responsibility.
Decision Engine may govern who should receive execution responsibility when the assignment itself requires an authorized choice.
A selected assignee is not automatically delegated until delegation is legitimately established.
Follow-Up Engine governs pursuit of missing information, approvals, or responses.
Decision Engine identifies what information or decision response is required.
A pending decision may require follow-up with the authorized decision-maker.
Decision Engine must not independently send follow-up communication.
Aging Engine governs unresolved duration, repeated deferral, and starvation.
Repeatedly deferred decisions may accumulate aging pressure.
Age alone does not determine the correct decision.
Chronic unresolved decisions may justify escalation or explicit disposition.
Escalation Engine determines when the decision requires higher or different authority.
Decision Engine determines the choice that requires resolution.
Not every important decision requires escalation.
Unknown or unavailable decision authority may justify escalation.
Resolution Engine governs terminal disposition.
A decision work item may resolve when an authorized decision is made and any required decision-specific closure criteria are satisfied.
Decision completion does not automatically resolve implementation work.
A cancelled decision must still satisfy Resolution Engine requirements.
Capture Engine may identify decision requirements from incoming information.
Decision Engine governs sufficiently supported operational decisions.
A selected decision may create new obligations requiring Capture Engine evaluation.
Decision Engine must not silently create unrelated work.
Reevaluation must preserve decision history.
Reevaluation should determine whether the decision remains required.
Reevaluation should refresh options and consequences from current supported information.
Material decision changes may trigger Priority, Attention, Dependency, Conflict, Capacity, Scheduling, Commitment, Delegation, Follow-Up, Aging, Escalation, or Resolution reevaluation.

requirements: Decision output must reference the applicable work_item_id.
Recommendation and authorized decision must remain distinguishable.
Unknown decision authority must remain unknown.
Option consequences must remain traceable and explainable where materially relevant.
Decision Engine must not directly overwrite canonical priority.
Material decision changes must be available to dependent operational engines.

guardrails: Do not convert every question into a decision.
Do not convert ordinary execution judgment into unnecessary approval bureaucracy.
Do not invent options merely to create the appearance of choice.
Do not present infeasible options as equally viable.
Do not represent a recommendation as the user's decision.
Do not silently modify commitments through a decision.
Do not silently delegate work through a decision.
Do not silently alter calendars through a decision.
Do not treat a made decision as implemented work.
Do not resolve downstream obligations merely because a decision was made.
Do not reopen decisions solely because hindsight makes another option look preferable.
Do not bypass the Attention Engine for user-facing presentation.
Do not bypass the Resolution Engine for terminal disposition.
Do not modify Core reasoning architecture as part of decision management.
